title: That the theology of wayfarers is taken in three ways; and that theology in the first sense is not a habit really distinct from faith
pass_a_gloss: Article XXIV. It is shown that the theology of wayfarers is taken in three ways; and it is proved that theology taken in the first way is not a habit really distinct from faith. 1. Wayfarers' theology is taken three ways: (1) for divine faith itself, by which we believe revealed mysteries; (2) for a scientific habit by which theological conclusions are deduced from faith's principles — as some Scholastics wish; (3) for an aggregate habit from faith and the philosophical disciplines, of which scholastic theology consists. 2. Theology in the first sense is not a habit really distinct from faith: it is faith itself, or faith's knowledge. Those who distinguish otherwise multiply habits without necessity.
pass_b_english: Article XXIV. That the theology of wayfarers is taken in three ways; and that theology in the first sense is not a habit really distinct from faith.

1. Wayfarers' theology three ways: (1) divine faith itself believing revealed mysteries; (2) a "scientific" habit deducing theological conclusions from faith's principles (some Scholastics); (3) an aggregate from faith and philosophy — scholastic theology.
2. In the first sense theology is not really distinct from faith — it is faith itself. Other distinctions multiply habits without need.
source_text:
ART. XXIV.
Ostenditur Theologiam Viatorum tribus modis accipi: & probatur Theologiam primo modo acceptam, non esse habitum a Fide re distinctum.

1. Theologia viatorum tribus modis accipitur: (1) pro ipsa fide divina, qua mysteria revelata credimus; (2) pro habitu scientifico quo ex principiis fidei conclusiones theologicae deducuntur — ut quidam Scholastici volunt; (3) pro habitu aggregato ex fide & disciplinis philosophicis, quo Scholastica Theologia constat.

2. Theologia primo modo accepta non est habitus a fide realiter distinctus: est ipsa fides, seu notitia fidei. Qui aliter distinguunt, multiplicant habitus sine necessitate.
